slides.kicker: It said five minutes. It was an hour.
slides.title:
Why does time
[[disappear]] when
I am not looking?
slides.sub: You are not careless. Your sense of time is just quiet.

slides.title:
There are only two
times: [[now]] and
not now
slides.body: Anything past "now" feels far away. A deadline next week has no weight at all — until the moment it becomes tomorrow.

slides.title:
You do not [[feel]]
time passing
slides.body: Most people carry a background sense of how long something has taken. With ADHD that sense is faint. An hour and five minutes can feel the same.

slides.title:
Every task looks
[[shorter]] than
it is
slides.body: "A quick shower" forgets the towel, the clothes, the hair. You plan for the middle of a task and lose the edges on either side.

slides.title:
Make time something
you can [[see]]
slides.body: A clock in every room. A visual timer that shows the minutes shrinking. If you cannot feel time, put it where your eyes already are.

slides.title:
[[Double]] your
first guess
slides.body: Estimate, then double it. Arriving early by accident is kinder to you than arriving late again.

slides.title:
Set the alarm for
the [[switch]], not
the event
slides.body: Not 3:00 for the meeting — 2:40 to stop what you are doing. Leaving the current thing is the hard part, so that is the moment to mark.

slides.title:
Count [[backwards]]
from the deadline
slides.body: Out the door at 8:30? Shoes at 8:25, bag at 8:20, showered by 8:00. One far-off time becomes several near ones you can actually feel.

slides.title:
Save this for the
next time an hour
[[vanishes]]
slides.body: Your clock is not broken, it is quiet. Make time loud enough to see. Dump the rest into my.adhd and get one thing back.
